claims.source: In neonates, motoneuron excitability was found to be increased (hyperexcitable) in some studies (van Zundert et al., 2008; Elbasiouny et al., 2010; Leroy et al., 2014), unaltered in others (Pambo-Pambo et al., 2009; Quinlan et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies showing no change in excitability.

claims.claim: A decrease in input resistance was reported in neonatal motoneurons, suggesting hypoexcitability.
claims.source: and in Bories et al. (2007), a decrease in input resistance was reported, suggesting that spinal motoneurons became hypoexcitable.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study showing decreased input resistance.

claims.claim: In adults before the onset of degeneration, a substantial fraction of motoneurons lose their ability to elicit a repetitive discharge in response to sustained inputs.
claims.source: At a later time point, in adults, before the onset of degeneration, we reported that a substantial fraction of motoneurons lose their ability to elicit a repetitive discharge in response to sustained inputs (Delestrée et al., 2014), a clear manifestation of hypoexcitability.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: The remaining motoneurons that still produced a repetitive discharge retained normal excitability.
claims.source: The remaining motoneurons, which still produced a repetitive discharge, retained normal excitability (Delestrée et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Studies in motoneurons derived from human iPSCs confirmed a tendency for excitability to shift from hyperexcitable to hypoexcitable during the course of the disease.
claims.source: Studies in motoneurons derived from human iPSCs confirmed this tendency for excitability to shift from a hyperexcitable (Wainger et al., 2014) to a hypoexcitable state (Sareen et al., 2014; Devlin et al., 2015; Naujock et al., 2016) during the course of the disease.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four studies on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claims.claim: The most vulnerable motoneurons in ALS are those of the largest motor units that innervate fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type).
claims.source: The most vulnerable and the first to degenerate are the motoneurons of the largest motor units that innervate the fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type), followed by the motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size, which innervate the fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on motor unit vulnerability.

claims.claim: Motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size that innervate fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type) degenerate after FF motoneurons.
claims.source: The most vulnerable and the first to degenerate are the motoneurons of the largest motor units that innervate the fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type), followed by the motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size, which innervate the fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on motor unit vulnerability patterns.

claims.claim: Motoneurons of the smallest motor units that mainly innervate slow contracting and fatigue-resistant fibers (S type) are the most resistant and least affected at end-stage disease.
claims.source: Finally, the motoneurons of the smallest motor units, that mainly innervate the slow contracting and fatigue-resistant fibers (S type) are the most resistant and the least affected at the end-stage of disease (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on motor unit vulnerability.

claims.claim: Only a subgroup of motoneurons are hyperexcitable (rheobase is lowered) at P6–P10 in mSOD1 mice.
claims.source: In a recent study, we demonstrated that only a subgroup of motoneurons are hyperexcitable (rheobase is lowered) at P6–P10 in mSOD1 mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: The hyperexcitable motoneurons at P6-P10 in mSOD1 mice were identified as S-type, the most resistant in ALS.
claims.source: However, using a combination of electrophysiological, morphological and molecular criteria, these motoneurons were identified as S-type, that is the most resistant in ALS (Leroy et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The intrinsic excitability of the most vulnerable motoneurons is unchanged at P6-P10 in mSOD1 mice.
claims.source: In sharp contrast, the intrinsic excitability of the most vulnerable motoneurons is unchanged at this age, arguing against the idea that early hyperexcitability contributes to selective degeneration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: FF motor units lose their neuromuscular junctions around 60 days post-natal in the SOD1G93A model.
claims.source: Nevertheless, degeneration of the most vulnerable motoneurons starts several weeks later (the FF motor units lose their neuromuscular junctions around 60 days post-natal in the SOD1G93A model; Pun et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on denervation timing.

claims.claim: Motoneurons that failed to discharge repetitively are distributed predominantly among the FF and the largest FR motor units.
claims.source: Our experiments revealed that motoneurons that failed to discharge repetitively in response to sustained inputs are distributed predominantly among the FF and the largest FR motor units.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: Large motor units tend to become hypoexcitable over disease progression in a mouse model of FUS-ALS.
claims.source: To do this, we repeated our experiments in a mouse model of FUS-ALS (Sharma et al., 2016) and found again that large motor units tend to become hypoexcitable over disease progression.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments in the FUS-ALS model.

claims.claim: Chodl has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons.
claims.source: Combining in vivo electrophysiology and in situ hybridization, we have investigated the expression pattern of C-type lectin chondrolectin (Chodl) in WT mice since it has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Chodl disappears over the course of ALS progression.
claims.source: Combining in vivo electrophysiology and in situ hybridization, we have investigated the expression pattern of C-type lectin chondrolectin (Chodl) in WT mice since it has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010) that disappears over the course of ALS progression (Wootz et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In WT mice, Chodl is expressed in FF motoneurons and in the largest FR motoneurons, but not in small FRs.
claims.source: In WT mice, we found that Chodl is expressed in the FF motoneurons, as well as in the largest FR motoneurons, but not in the small FRs, matching the hypoexcitability pattern in SOD1G93A mice.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments combining electrophysiology and in situ hybridization.

claims.claim: FR motoneurons constitute a heterogeneous population that differentially lose their ability to fire repetitively over the course of disease progression.
claims.source: Altogether, our data indicate that FR motoneurons constitute a heterogeneous population that differentially lose their ability to fire repetitively over the course of disease progression, a property that may underlie their differential vulnerability in ALS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on FR motoneuron properties.

claims.claim: The expression patterns of p-eIF2α and p62 aggregates suggest that hypoexcitable motoneurons are more advanced in disease progression than those that still fire repetitively.
claims.source: Moreover, the expression patterns of p-eIF2α and p62 aggregates suggest that the hypoexcitable motoneurons are more advanced in the disease progression than those that still fire repetitively.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunostaining data on disease markers.

claims.claim: In ALS mice, both FF and the largest FR motoneurons lose the fundamental property of firing repetitively prior to their degeneration.
claims.source: We conclude that in ALS mice, both the FF and the largest FR motoneurons are not hyperexcitable prior to their degeneration, but on the contrary, lose the fundamental property of firing repetitively.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Recordings were performed on 46 to 60 days old animals (WT: 54 ± 5 days; N = 45; SOD1G93A: 52 ± 5 days; N = 36).
claims.source: Recordings were performed on 46 to 60 days old animals (WT: 54 ± 5 days; N = 45; SOD1G93A: 52 ± 5 days; N = 36).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claims.claim: The contractile properties (twitch amplitude, twitch contraction time and fatigue index) vary widely across the motor unit population but display inter-relationships in both WT and SOD1G93A animals.
claims.source: Figure 2 shows that, despite the fact that the contractile properties (namely twitch amplitude, twitch contraction time and fatigue index) vary widely across the motor unit population, they clearly display some inter-relationships in both WT and SOD1G93A animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A cutoff value of 20 ms was used to separate 'slow' motor units from 'fast' contracting ones.
claims.source: We chose a cutoff value of 20 ms to separate those 'slow' motor units from the 'fast' contracting ones.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the data distribution.

claims.claim: All motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms developed a weak twitch force (all but one under 1.0 mN).
claims.source: Indeed, all the motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms developed a weak twitch force (all but one under 1.0 mN: WT: 0.7 ± 0.5 mN; [0.2–1.8 mN]; N = 8; SOD1G93A: 0.4 ± 0.3 mN; [0.1–1.1 mN]; N = 12; Figure 2A1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 2A1.

claims.claim: Fast motor units (contraction time shorter than 20 ms) displayed a much wider range of twitch force.
claims.source: In contrast, the fast motor units (contraction time shorter than 20 ms) displayed a much wider range of twitch force (WT: 3.8 ± 5.4 mN; [0.1–29.8 mN]; N = 98; SOD1G93A: 5.9 ± 10.3 mN; [0.1–53.1 mN]; N = 80; Figure 2A1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 2A1.

claims.claim: Motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms were all fatigue resistant (fatigue index between 0.86 and 1.00 in both WT and SOD1G93A mice).
claims.source: Motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms were all fatigue resistant (fatigue index between 0.86 and 1.00 in both WT and SOD1G93A mice, Figure 2A2 and B2; see also the slow-contracting motor unit in Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A2, 2B2, and 1C.

claims.claim: All of the fatigable motor units (fatigue index below 0.5) developed a large initial amount of twitch force.
claims.source: However, all of the fatigable motor units (fatigue index below 0.5) developed a large initial amount of twitch force (e.g. 12.7 mN for the motor unit in Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data and an example from Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Fast-contracting, fatigue resistant (FR) units can be distinguished from fast-contracting, fatigable (FF) units using a cut-off value of 8 mN.
claims.source: Remarkably, with very few exceptions, we were able to distinguish fast contracting, fatigue resistant (FR) from fast-contracting, fatigable (FF) units a cut-off value of 8 mN (Figure 2A3 and B3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A3 and 2B3.

claims.claim: In WT mice, 13 motor units were classified as FF (12%), 85 as FR (80%) and eight as S (8%).
claims.source: In WT mice, we classified 13 motor units as FF (12%), 85 as FR (80%) and eight as S (8%).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the classification results from the study.

claims.claim: In SOD1G93A mice, 15 units were classified as FF (16%), 65 as FR (71%) and 12 as S (13%).
claims.source: In SOD1G93A mice, we classified 15 units as FF (16%), 65 as FR (71%) and 12 as S (13%).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the classification results from the study.

claims.claim: The proportions of motor units of each type found in WT vs. SOD1G93A mice were not statistically different.
claims.source: The proportions of motor units of each type found in WT vs. SOD1G93A mice were not statistically different (χ2 test p=0.28)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: FF motor units display a slightly longer contraction time in mutant mice.
claims.source: We observed that FF motor units display a slightly longer contraction time in mutant mice.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claims.claim: The longer contraction time in FF motor units might reflect a desynchronization of their muscle fibers that precedes denervation proper.
claims.source: Since these units develop a similar amount of force as in control mice (Table 1), this might reflect a desynchronization of their muscle fibers that precedes denervation proper.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of SOD1G93A motoneurons was not able to discharge in response to a ramp, despite being able to fire at the onset of a square pulse.
claims.source: As we previously described (Delestrée et al., 2014), a substantial fraction of motoneurons was not able to discharge in response to the ramp, despite the fact that they were still able to fire at the onset of a square pulse (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The loss of repetitive firing is a manifestation of hypoexcitability of motoneurons.
claims.source: This lack of repetitive firing is a manifestation of hypoexcitability of these motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on established understanding of neuronal excitability.

claims.claim: The loss of function occurs before the denervation of the neuromuscular junctions.
claims.source: Notably, this loss of function occurs before the denervation of the neuromuscular junctions as every cell in this study was able to activate its muscle fibers (as shown by the recording of a motor unit action potential at the surface of the muscle) and to produce a twitch in response to a spike elicited by a short pulse of current (Figure 3A2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing functional neuromuscular junctions.

claims.claim: The loss of function was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (21% vs. 6%).
claims.source: The loss of function was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (21% vs. 6%, exact Fisher test p=0.01, Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Non-firing motoneurons were more prevalent in the largest motor units.
claims.source: Moreover, non-firing motoneurons were not distributed homogeneously in all physiological types of motor units, but were more prevalent in the largest units (Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: In SOD1G93A mice, 40% of the FF units (6/15 tested) were unable to fire repetitively.
claims.source: In SOD1G93A mice, 40% of the FF units (6/15 tested) were unable to fire repetitively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: Among FR units in SOD1G93A mice, 20% (11/55 tested) were unable to fire repetitively, but all non-firing cells were among the largest FR motor units (1.5–4.0 mN).
claims.source: Among the FR units, 20% (11/55 tested) were unable to fire repetitively, but all the non-firing cells were among the largest FR motor unit (1.5–4.0 mN)
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: 46% of the large FR units (11/24 tested) in SOD1G93A mice were unable to fire repetitively.
claims.source: if we split the FR population in two along the median (1.3 mN), 46% of the large FR (11/24 tested) were unable to fire repetitively
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: 100% of the small FR units in SOD1G93A mice fired repetitively (31/31 tested).
claims.source: whereas 100% of the small FR units fired repetitively (31/31 tested).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: All S units in SOD1G93A mice were able to fire repetitively (8/8 tested).
claims.source: Similarly, all the S units were able to fire repetitively (8/8 tested).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claims.claim: The motor units that did not fire repetitively developed significantly more force than those that were able to fire repetitively, regardless of genotype.
claims.source: ANOVA analysis confirmed that the motor units that did not fire repetitively developed significantly more force than those that were able to fire repetitively, regardless of the genotype (p<0.001, Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The motoneurons' input conductances were, on average, larger in FF motor units than in FRs, which were in turn larger than in slow motoneurons.
claims.source: As expected, the motoneurons' input conductances were, on average, larger in FF motor units than in FRs, which were in turn larger than in slow motoneurons (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: The motoneurons that were unable to discharge repetitively had a larger input conductance than those that still fired repetitively, regardless of genotype.
claims.source: The motoneurons that were unable to discharge repetitively had a larger input conductance than those that still fired repetitively, regardless of the genotype (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001; Figure 3G)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The motoneurons that did not fire repetitively had an average resting membrane potential more depolarized than those that did, regardless of genotype.
claims.source: Interestingly, the motoneurons that did not fire repetitively had an average resting membrane potential more depolarized than those that did, regardless of their genotype (two-way ANOVA, p=0.01)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Non-repetitively-firing SOD1G93A motoneurons had an average resting membrane potential of −62 ± 8 mV (N = 17).
claims.source: non-repetitively-firing SOD1G93A motoneurons had an average resting membrane potential of −62 ± 8 mV (N = 17)
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claims.claim: SOD1G93A motoneurons that fired repetitively rested at −68 ± 8 mV (N = 63).
claims.source: while those that fired repetitively rested at −68 ± 8 mV (N = 63)(Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The largest motor units (FF and FR larger than 1.3 mN) were more depolarized in SOD1G93A mice than in controls.
claims.source: Overall, we observed that the largest motor units (FF and FR larger than 1.3 mN) were more depolarized in SOD1G93A mice than in controls (Table 2)
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: The recruitment current is linearly related to the input conductance of the motoneuron.
claims.source: The recruitment current is linearly related to the input conductance of the motoneuron: the larger the input conductance, the larger the recruitment current (Figure 4A, r2 = 0.81, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The recruitment current was on average larger in FF motoneurons than in FRs, which was in turn larger than in S motoneurons.
claims.source: Therefore, similarly to the input conductance, the recruitment current was on average larger in the FF motoneurons than in the FRs, where it was, in turn, larger than in the S motoneurons (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p<0.0001; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: The recruitment current was unchanged for all motoneuron types in SOD1G93A mice compared with WT mice.
claims.source: Compared with WT mice, the recruitment current was unchanged for all motoneuron types in SOD1G93A mice compared with the WT mice (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: The slope of the relationship between recruitment current and input conductance was not significantly different between WT and SOD1G93A motoneurons.
claims.source: Comparing WT and SOD1G93A motoneurons, we found that the slope of the relationship between the recruitment current and the input conductance was not significantly different (ANCOVA p=0.99, Figure 4A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The excitability of motoneurons that retain the ability to fire repetitively was unaffected by the mutation.
claims.source: indicating that the excitability of the motoneurons that retain the ability to fire repetitively was unaffected by the mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of recruitment current data.

claims.claim: The voltage excursion was unaffected in SOD1G93A vs. WT motoneurons.
claims.source: The voltage excursion (difference between the spiking voltage threshold and the resting membrane potential) was also unaffected in SOD1G93A vs. WT motoneurons (WT: 17.4 ± 7.3 mV; N = 48 vs. SOD1G93A: 18.2 ± 5.3 mV; N = 56; Mann-Whitney p=0.64; Figure 4C; and Table 2 for the distributions among motoneuron types).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claims.claim: The gain (slope of frequency-current relationship in primary range) was unchanged in the whole population of motoneurons that fired during the ramp.
claims.source: In the whole population of motoneurons that fired during the ramp, we found that the gain was unchanged (WT: 14 ± 6 Hz/nA; N = 43 vs. SOD1G93A: 17 ± 9 Hz/nA; N = 54 Mann-Whitney p=0.10; Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The motoneurons that become hypoexcitable by losing the ability to fire repetitively all belong to the FF motor units or the largest FR motor units.
claims.source: Overall, our results show that the motoneurons that become hypoexcitable by losing the ability to fire repetitively all belong to the FF motor units or the largest FR motor units
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The remaining SOD1G93A motoneurons retain their normal excitability.
claims.source: whereas the remaining SOD1G93A motoneurons retain their normal excitability.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the excitability measurements.

claims.claim: Denervation of Tibialis Anterior (TA) in the τONFUSP525L mouse precedes denervation of TS.
claims.source: In contrast to the SOD1G93A model, where denervation occurs fairly synchronously across hindlimb motor pools (Pun et al., 2006), denervation of Tibialis Anterior (TA, an ankle flexor muscle) in the 𝜏ONFUSP525L mouse precedes denervation of TS (an ankle extensor)(Sharma et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claims.claim: The progression of denervation is much slower in τONFUSP525L than in SOD1G93A mice.
claims.source: Moreover, the progression of the denervation is much slower in 𝜏ONFUSP525L than in SOD1G93A mice.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on the cited literature.

claims.claim: The TS motor unit properties in FUS mice were remarkably similar to those recorded in the SOD1G93A mouse, regardless of age.
claims.source: Despite some small variations in twitch amplitudes, the TS motor unit properties were remarkably similar to those recorded in the SOD1G93A mouse, regardless of the age (compare Figure 2A–B and Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claims.claim: Motor units recorded from ankle flexors were all fast-contracting.
claims.source: Consistent with the fact that TA and EDL are almost devoid of Type I muscle fibers (Wang and Kernell, 2001; Bloemberg and Quadrilatero, 2012), motor units recorded from the ankle flexors were all fast-contracting
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental observations.

claims.claim: A large proportion of motoneurons in τONFUSP525L mice did not fire repetitively in response to a slow ramp of current.
claims.source: As in SOD1G93A mice, we observed a large proportion of motoneurons in 𝜏ONFUSP525L mice that did not fire repetitively in response to a slow ramp of current (Figure 5A1)
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5A1.

claims.claim: The loss of function in FUSP525L mice occurred at a time when the neuromuscular junctions are not denervated.
claims.source: Again, this loss of function occurred at a time when the neuromuscular junctions are not denervated, as shown by the fact that an action potential elicited by a transient electrical pulse in the cell body elicits a motor unit action potential and a twitch of the motor unit (Figure 5A2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A2.

claims.claim: In ankle extensor motor pools, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different between WT and mutant animals at P30 or P180.
claims.source: In the ankle extensor motor pools, where denervation is the slowest, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different between WT and mutant animals at either time point studied (Fisher exact test, p=0.69 at P30, p=1.00 at P180).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: In ankle flexor motor pools at P30, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically significant between FUSP525L and FUSWT mice.
claims.source: In the ankle flexor motor pools, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically significant at P30, when the denervation is just starting (Fisher exact test, p=0.43).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: At P180, there were significantly more non-repetitively-firing motoneurons in FUSP525L than in FUSWT mice (42% vs. 18%).
claims.source: However, at P180, when the denervation is more advanced, there were significantly more non-repetitively-firing motoneurons in FUSP525L than in FUSWT mice (42% vs. 18%, respectively; Fisher exact test, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: In FF units of FUSP525L mice, 7/9 (78%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively.
claims.source: In FF units, we found that 7/9 (78%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively (vs. 2/7, 17% in WT mice; Fisher exact test p=0.04).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In FR units of FUSP525L mice, 7/22 (32%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively, which was not statistically different from WT mice.
claims.source: In FR units (large and small taken together), we found that only 7/22 (32%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively, which was not statistically different from WT mice (4/21, 19%; Fisher exact test p=0.49).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The proportion of non-firing motoneurons was much larger in large ankle flexor motor units in FUSP525L vs. FUSWT mice at P180 (13/19, 68% vs. 3/17, 18%).
claims.source: when we split our samples between 'large' and 'small' motor units (based on the same cutoff value of 1.3 mN as used above, which is also the median twitch amplitude of FR ankle flexor units), the proportion of non-firing motoneuron was much larger in the large ankle flexor motor units in FUSP525L vs. FUSWT mice at P180 (13/19, 68% vs. 3/17, 18%, respectively; Fisher exact test, p=0.003)
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different in small motor units between FUSP525L and FUSWT mice (WT: 2/10, 20% vs. FUS: 1/12, 8%).
claims.source: whereas the proportion was not statistacally different in the small motor units (WT: 2/10, 20% vs. FUS: 1/12, 8%; Fisher exact test, p=0.57).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The resting membrane potential of ankle flexor motoneurons at P180 tended to be more depolarized in non-firing cells than in cells able to fire repetitively, regardless of phenotype.
claims.source: we observed that the resting membrane potential of ankle flexor motoneurons at P180 tended to be more depolarized in non-firing cells than in cells able to fire repetitively, regardless of the phenotype (FUSWT: non-firing −60 ± 7 mV; N = 6 vs. firing −72 ± 6 mV; N = 28; FUSP525L: non-firing −65 ± 7 mV; N = 15 vs. firing −70 ± 10 mV; N = 21; two-way ANOVA, p=0.001; Figure 6A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The ankle flexor motoneurons that were able to fire repetitively at P180 retained normal excitability in FUSP525L mice.
claims.source: Also in keeping with our results in the SOD1 model, the ankle flexor motoneurons that were able to fire repetitively at P180 retained normal excitability.

results.result: Motor units in WT and SOD1G93A mice were classified into FF, FR, and S types based on contractile properties (twitch amplitude, contraction time, fatigue index). The classification used cutoff values of 20 ms for contraction time and 8 mN for twitch force. The proportions of motor unit types were similar between WT and SOD1G93A mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C37 provide comprehensive methodological details and quantitative data for motor unit classification. The classification scheme is well-justified by the data shown in Figures 1-2, with clear cutoff values and statistical validation (χ² test p=0.28). The inter-relationships between contractile properties support the validity of the classification approach.

results.result: In SOD1G93A mice, motoneurons innervating FF and large FR motor units (>1.3 mN) lose the ability to fire repetitively before denervation of neuromuscular junctions. This hypoexcitability was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A (21%) than WT (6%) mice, with 40% of FF units and 46% of large FR units affected, while all small FR and S units retained repetitive firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C40-C50, C64 collectively demonstrate selective hypoexcitability in vulnerable motor units with strong statistical support (Fisher exact test p=0.01, ANOVA p<0.001). The data clearly show that loss of repetitive firing occurs before denervation (C42) and is selective for large motor units (C44-C49), supported by Figures 3D-F.

results.result: Non-repetitively firing motoneurons had larger input conductances and more depolarized resting membrane potentials than repetitively firing motoneurons. In SOD1G93A mice, non-firing motoneurons rested at −62±8 mV versus −68±8 mV for firing motoneurons, and the largest motor units were more depolarized in mutants than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 for input conductance, p=0.01 for membrane potential) and data in Figure 3G-H and Table 2. The findings are internally consistent and link electrophysiological properties to firing capability.

results.result: Motoneurons that retained repetitive firing capability showed normal excitability in SOD1G93A mice. Recruitment current, voltage excursion, and gain were unchanged compared to WT mice, with the slope of the recruitment current-input conductance relationship unaffected (ANCOVA p=0.99).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63, C65 demonstrate preserved excitability in firing motoneurons with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney, ANCOVA) and data in Figure 4 and Table 2. The linear relationship between recruitment current and input conductance (r²=0.81, p<0.0001) supports the validity of the measurements.

results.result: In the FUS-ALS model (τONFUSP525L mice), large motor units showed progressive hypoexcitability similar to SOD1G93A mice. At P180 in ankle flexors, 68% of large motor units (>1.3 mN) in FUSP525L mice were non-firing versus 18% in controls (p=0.003), while small motor units were unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C66-C78 demonstrate that hypoexcitability is not specific to SOD1 mutations, supported by statistical analyses (Fisher exact tests) and data in Figure 5. The temporal and motor pool-specific patterns strengthen the generalizability of the findings, though the sample sizes for some comparisons are modest.

results.result: In FUSP525L mice at P180, non-firing ankle flexor motoneurons had more depolarized resting potentials than firing motoneurons (two-way ANOVA p=0.001), while firing motoneurons retained normal excitability with unchanged recruitment current and input conductance relationship (ANCOVA p=0.19).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by statistical analyses and data in Figure 6, confirming that the pattern observed in SOD1G93A mice generalizes to the FUS model. The consistency across models strengthens the overall conclusions.

results.result: Chodl expression in WT mice was selective for FF motoneurons and large FR motoneurons (>1.3 mN), with 8/9 large motor units expressing Chodl versus 2/10 small motor units. Chodl+ motor units developed significantly more force (8.1±8.6 mN) than Chodl− units (0.8±0.6 mN, p<0.0001), indicating FR motoneurons comprise two distinct subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C83-C88 combine electrophysiology with molecular markers to demonstrate FR heterogeneity. The data in Figure 7 show clear separation between Chodl+ and Chodl− populations with strong statistical support. However, the sample size is modest (N=19 motoneurons), and the correlation with hypoexcitability pattern is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Disease marker analysis showed that non-firing motoneurons had lower p-eIF2α levels (0.2±0.2) than firing motoneurons (0.8±0.2, p=0.02), while p62 aggregates were variable but high in some non-firing cells. This pattern suggests non-firing motoneurons are at a more advanced disease stage than firing motoneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C103 provide important mechanistic insights, but the sample size is very small (N=8 motoneurons total, 4 firing and 4 non-firing from 6 mice). The p-eIF2α finding is statistically significant but based on minimal replication. The p62 data are more variable and less conclusive (C101-C102). While the interpretation is plausible given prior literature (C92), the limited sample size and variability in p62 expression warrant caution.

results.result: The study concludes that intrinsic hyperexcitability is unlikely to cause motoneuron degeneration in ALS. Instead, hypoexcitability (loss of repetitive firing) precedes denervation and represents an early sign of degeneration, with this mechanism generalizing across two unrelated ALS models.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26, C105, C126 represent the main conclusions, well-supported by the convergent evidence from SOD1G93A and FUSP525L models (C2, C19, C20, C42, C64). The demonstration that hypoexcitability occurs before denervation in vulnerable motor units across two models provides strong support for this conclusion.

results.result: Prior literature shows conflicting evidence on motoneuron excitability in ALS models, with hyperexcitability reported in embryonic and some neonatal stages, but hypoexcitability emerging in adults. The most vulnerable motoneurons (FF type) are the first to degenerate, followed by FR, with S-type being most resistant.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C18 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the context and rationale for the current study, highlighting the controversy about excitability changes and the selective vulnerability of motor unit types.

results.result: FF motor units in SOD1G93A mice displayed slightly longer contraction times than in WT mice, which might reflect desynchronization of muscle fibers preceding denervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by data in Table 1 showing statistically significant differences (p=0.005). However, C39 is speculative about the mechanism. The observation is valid but the interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: This is the first study in a mouse model of ALS to correlate changes in electrical properties of motoneurons with the physiological type of their motor unit.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is a statement about the novelty of the approach. The methodology combining in vivo intracellular recording with motor unit characterization in non-paralyzed mice is indeed novel for ALS models, as supported by the methodological descriptions and citations.

results.result: Loss of repetitive firing develops progressively during ALS, with 35% of motoneurons affected by P30-P60. This loss is unrelated to anesthesia and parallels findings in iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patients, which transition from hyperexcitable to hypoexcitable over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C112 integrate current findings with prior work (citations to Delestrée et al., 2014 and iPSC studies). The consistency across mouse models and human iPSC-derived neurons strengthens the translational relevance, though these are primarily literature-based claims.

results.result: Mechanistic hypotheses suggest that loss of repetitive firing may result from insufficient persistent sodium current, imbalance in sodium/potassium currents, or membrane depolarization due to reduced ATP availability. Theoretical modeling suggests membrane depolarization is greatest at distal axon and decreasing firing rate may be compensatory to prevent energy crisis.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C120 present mechanistic hypotheses based on literature (citations to Delestrée, Huh, Sareen, Devlin, Naujock, Le Masson studies). While these are plausible mechanisms consistent with the observations, they are not directly tested in this study. The claims appropriately use speculative language (C113, C120) but represent inferences rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

results.result: Pharmacological and chemogenetic studies suggest that modulating excitability has therapeutic potential: early enhancement of excitability or late reduction of hypoexcitability may be beneficial, supporting a model where hypoexcitability contributes to motoneuron degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 summarize prior therapeutic studies (Wainger, Naujock, Saxena) that support the functional significance of excitability changes. These literature-based claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings, though they do not represent new data from this study.
